problem_statement: The paper frames the task as pricing European-style financial derivatives, especially vanilla options, by solving the Black-Scholes equation for the option price dynamics. It also notes that numerical solutions are important for hedging portfolios with many coupled options.
problem_statement_quotes:
Pricing financial derivatives, in particular European-style options at different time-maturities and strikes,
means a relevant problem in finance.
One of the fundamental tasks of quantitative finance is to calculate a fair price of such option contract before its expiration time.

Besides, numerical solutions also turn out to be fundamental when hedg-
ing a portfolio with a great number of coupled options.
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical option-pricing approaches as solving the Black-Scholes PDE with standard numerical methods, and it contrasts its approach with Monte Carlo methods that sample the solution. It also lists finite differences, finite elements, Monte Carlo methods, and Fourier spectral methods as classical methods in the literature.
classical_baseline_quotes:
Our approach differs from those based on Monte Carlo integration, exclusively focused on sampling the solu-
tion assuming the dynamics is known.

In comparison with previous methods, our algo-
rithm presents a Hamiltonian simulation methodology to solve the Black-Scholes partial differential equation instead of solv-
ing the stochastic differential equation.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the pricing task is not straightforward because the underlying stock and interest rates evolve randomly, and that the Black-Scholes Hamiltonian is non-Hermitian, which makes direct simulation on a quantum computer challenging. It also states that arbitrary state loading can require an exponential number of gates, and that without periodic-boundary-compatible diagonalization one can incur exponential cost in the general case.
classical_difficulty_quotes:

the interest rates, whose dynamics can be modelled via either

extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract and introduction; paper is focused on derivative pricing and contrasts with Monte Carlo and classical PDE solvers.
